content:
When arthritis makes cooking, opening packets or chewing hard work, protein is often the first thing to drop, and muscle strength goes with it. You do not need to cook from scratch: eggs, tinned fish, beans and lentils, cheese, yoghurt, milk, nut butters, ready-cooked chicken and frozen ready meals all count. Aim for some protein at every meal and snack, little and often. If you are eating less or losing weight without trying, ask your GP to check your weight and refer you to a dietitian. Do not start protein shakes or supplements without checking first if you have kidney disease or swallowing problems. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

This guide is about getting enough protein when your hands, energy or teeth make food hard work. For how much protein people with arthritis need and the best sources, see protein and arthritis: how much you need. If you have simply gone off your food, see appetite loss and arthritis.

Why protein matters more when moving is hard

Muscles help protect painful joints and keep you steady on your feet. When you eat less, especially protein, and move less, muscle is lost more quickly. The NHS says people aged 65 and over are particularly at risk of malnutrition, and that weight loss is not an inevitable part of getting older. Eating enough protein works best alongside gentle strength exercise. See seated strength exercises.

No-cook and low-effort protein

  • Dairy: milk, yoghurt, fromage frais, cheese, cottage cheese and milky puddings such as rice pudding or custard.
  • Eggs: boiled in batches and kept in the fridge, scrambled in the microwave, or bought ready-boiled.
  • Tins: tuna, salmon, sardines, mackerel, baked beans, chickpeas, lentils and soups with beans or meat.
  • Ready-cooked: sliced chicken or ham, rotisserie chicken, fish fillets in sauce that cook in the bag, frozen ready meals and fish fingers.
  • Snacks: nut butter on toast or crackers, hummus, a handful of nuts if chewing is fine, cheese and crackers, a glass of milk.

Making it easier on painful hands

  • Choose ring-pull tins, or use an electric tin opener or a jar opener.
  • Buy food ready-chopped, grated or sliced, and use a microwave rather than the hob where you can.
  • Sit down to prepare food, and keep the things you use most at waist height.
  • Cook once and freeze portions on a good day.
  • Ask an occupational therapist about kitchen equipment. Your council can do a free care needs assessment, which can include help with meals or equipment. Some areas also have meal delivery services.

For more ideas, see cooking with arthritis and our diet guide.

If chewing or swallowing is hard

Softer protein foods include scrambled eggs, flaked fish in sauce, mince, lentil soup, yoghurt, milky drinks and smooth nut butters. If you have a sore mouth or dentures that do not fit, see your dentist. If you cough or choke when eating or drinking, or food feels stuck, see your GP: the NHS says swallowing problems need checking, and a speech and language therapist can advise on safe textures.

Little and often

If big meals feel too much, eat smaller amounts more often and include protein each time. The NHS says the first advice for someone at risk of malnutrition is usually to eat foods fortified with extra calories and protein, snack between meals and have nourishing drinks. Simple ways to fortify food include adding grated cheese to soup or mash, stirring milk powder into milk or porridge, and having a milky drink instead of a cup of tea.

Supplements and shakes: check first

Most people can get enough protein from ordinary food. Do not buy protein powders or supplement drinks without asking your GP, pharmacist or a dietitian first, particularly if you have kidney disease, diabetes or swallowing problems. If your GP or dietitian thinks you need nutritional drinks, they can prescribe them. If you have gout, ask before making big changes, as some high-protein foods such as red meat, offal and some seafood can trigger attacks. See gout and diet.

When to get help

  • See your GP if you or someone you care for is losing weight without trying, clothes or rings have become loose, or eating has dropped off for more than a week or two. They can check your weight and refer you to a dietitian.
  • Get urgent advice from NHS 111 if someone is barely eating or drinking, is passing very little urine, or seems more unwell than usual.
  • Call 999 if someone is choking and cannot breathe, or is suddenly confused or very drowsy.

For family and carers

Notice what is actually being eaten, not just what is bought. Stock easy protein foods at the front of the fridge, open stiff packaging in advance, and share a meal when you can. Eating with someone often helps appetite.

Common questions

Can protein help my joints directly?

Protein does not repair arthritic joints, but it helps keep your muscles strong, which supports your joints and your balance. It works best with regular gentle exercise.

Are plant proteins as good?

Beans, lentils, chickpeas, tofu, nuts and seeds are all good sources. Mixing different ones through the day helps.

Should I take vitamin D too?

The NHS advises everyone in the UK to consider a daily vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter, and some people all year round, including those who rarely go outside. Check with your pharmacist if you take other medicines.
